name: Level 1: A1 Fondamenta
description: Master the 2 foundational pillars (Essere & Avere), articles, and preposition contractions.

lessons.title: The Two Pillars: Essere & Avere
lessons.subtitle: Why these two irregular verbs are the engine of all Italian sentences.
lessons.mentalModel: Just like 'To Be' and 'To Have' in English, Italian relies entirely on Essere and Avere. They describe identity, state, and possession—and in Level 2, they act as the auxiliary 'helpers' for every past tense action!

concepts.it: io sono / lui è / loro sono
concepts.en: I am / he (she) is / they are (Essere)
concepts.note: Notice 'è' (is with accent). Without accent, 'e' means 'and'.

concepts.it: io ho / lui ha / loro hanno
concepts.en: I have / he (she) has / they have (Avere)
concepts.note: The 'h' in Italian is silent! 'ha' sounds like 'ah'.

xray.fullEn: The friend is at home and has a book.

lessons.bridgeMarker: Golden Bridge to Level 4 (YDS): Keep an eye on Essere! In formal YDS sentences, its 3rd-person subjunctive form becomes sia (singular) and siano (plural)—which you saw earlier! And its past form becomes è stato (was). When you see 'siano' on the YDS, you are simply looking at essere!

checkQuiz.question: How do you say 'The researchers have' in Italian?
checkQuiz.explanation: For plural subjects ('loro' / they), 'avere' conjugates as 'hanno'.

lessons.title: Articles & Preposition Contractions
lessons.subtitle: How prepositions combine with articles (in + il = nel, di + la = della).
lessons.mentalModel: Every Italian noun has a grammatical gender: 🔴 Feminine (Red) or 🔵 Masculine (Blue). Recognizing the article instantly reveals the gender and how prepositions will contract around it!

concepts.en: 🔵 MASCULINE (Blue): il libro (i libri), lo studente (gli studenti), l'amico (gli amici)
concepts.note: Use 'lo' before s+consonant, z, gn; use 'l'' before vowels.

concepts.en: 🔴 FEMININE (Red): la casa (le case), l'idea (le idee)
concepts.note: Feminine nouns almost always end in -a (plural -e).

concepts.it: in + il = nel / in + la = nella
concepts.en: Contractions: in the (masculine blue: nel / feminine red: nella)
concepts.note: nel libro (in the book), nella società (in society)

concepts.it: di + il = del / di + la = della
concepts.note: la struttura del progetto, la voce della scienza

concepts.it: da + il = dal / da + la = dalla
concepts.en: Contractions: from / by the (agent in passive: dal / dalla / dagli)

xray.fullEn: The research is in the desk drawer.

lessons.bridgeMarker: Golden Bridge to Level 4 (YDS): In YDS passive voice questions, actions are carried out by someone using da + article (e.g. 'è stato scoperto dagli esperti' = was discovered by the experts). Spotting 'dagli' gives you the subject instantly!

lessons.title: The Present Tense Verb Rhythm
lessons.subtitle: The 3 regular endings (-are, -ere, -ire) and the vital 3rd-person rule.
lessons.mentalModel: Italian verbs belong to three families based on their infinitives: -are (parlare), -ere (leggere), and -ire (dormire). For academic reading, 95% of verbs are 3rd-person singular (-a/-e) or plural (-ano/-ono)!

concepts.note: Singular ends in -a; plural ends in -ano.
Singular ends in -e; plural ends in -ono.
Singular ends in -e; plural ends in -ono.

xray.fullEn: The students read and write together.

lessons.bridgeMarker: Golden Bridge to Level 4 (YDS): Notice that all plural verbs end in -no (parlano, scrivono, sono, hanno). On YDS translation questions, checking if the verb ends in '-no' immediately eliminates singular distractors!

checkQuiz.question: Which ending indicates 3rd-person PLURAL (they) in Italian?
checkQuiz.explanation: All 3rd-person plural verbs end in -no (they speak, they write, they are).

lessons.title: The Core Irregular Action Verbs: Fare & Andare
lessons.subtitle: Mastering the two most frequent action drivers in Italian sentences.
lessons.mentalModel: Just like 'to do/make' and 'to go' in English, Italian uses fare (fa, fanno) and andare (va, vanno) constantly. Notice how the 3rd-person forms still end in -a (singular) and -anno (plural)!

concepts.note: fa una ricerca (conducts research), fa parte di (is part of)
va verso (goes toward), vanno a Roma (they go to Rome)

xray.fullEn: The scientist makes an important discovery.

lessons.bridgeMarker: Bridge to YDS: 'Fare' is used in academic Italian for expressions like 'fare riferimento a' (to refer to) and 'fare parte di' (to belong to).

checkQuiz.question: How do you say 'The researchers conduct (make) research'?

lessons.title: Venire & Dare: Motion & Passive Foundation
lessons.subtitle: How 'Venire' acts as a passive engine and 'Dare' provides results.
lessons.mentalModel: Venire (viene, vengono) means 'to come', but in academic Italian it has a superpower: it is used as a passive auxiliary (*viene considerato* = is considered)! Dare (dà, danno) means 'to give'.

concepts.note: Later in Level 3: viene fatto = is done!

lessons.bridgeMarker: YDS Secret: In Level 3, you will see 'viene' replacing 'è' in passive sentences: 'Il testo viene tradotto' = 'The text is translated'.

checkQuiz.question: What is the 3rd person singular of Venire?

lessons.title: Negation & Invariable Markers
lessons.subtitle: Non, mai, nulla, niente: How Italian handles negative statements.
lessons.mentalModel: Italian uses a double negative naturally: non goes before the verb (*Non abbiamo tempo*). With 'mai' (never), 'non ... mai' forms complete negation.

concepts.note: non è più valido (is no longer valid)

lessons.bridgeMarker: YDS Trap: 'Non solo ... ma anche' means 'Not only ... but also', a very frequent connector pairing on YDS!

checkQuiz.question: Where does 'non' go in an Italian sentence?

options.text: At the very end of the sentence

lessons.title: Interrogative Question Stems
lessons.subtitle: Chi, cosa, dove, quando, perché, come, quanto.
lessons.mentalModel: These words question subjects, objects, reasons, and times. Crucial for understanding Reading Comprehension question stems on exams!
lessons.bridgeMarker: Exam Skill: Reading question stems always begin with these words (e.g. *Secondo il testo, perché...?* = According to the text, why...?).

checkQuiz.question: What does 'Perché' mean in Italian?
checkQuiz.explanation: 'Perché' handles both the question (why) and the answer (because).

lessons.title: Adjectives & Agreement Rules
lessons.subtitle: How Italian adjectives adapt to masculine, feminine, and plural nouns.
lessons.mentalModel: Unlike English where 'big' never changes, Italian adjectives match the noun: *un buon libro* -> *buoni libri*; *una buona idea* -> *buone idee*.
lessons.bridgeMarker: Elimination Hack: Match the adjective's gender/number with the subject to quickly eliminate 2 out of 5 options on YDS!

checkQuiz.question: What is the plural of 'importante'?
checkQuiz.explanation: Adjectives ending in -e change to -i in the plural for both masculine and feminine.

lessons.title: Possession & Attribution
lessons.subtitle: Il suo, la sua, i loro: Tracking who owns what in academic texts.
lessons.mentalModel: Italian puts the definite article before possessives: *la sua ricerca* (his/her research), *i loro risultati* (their results).
lessons.bridgeMarker: Academic Reading: 'Il loro' never changes its ending! Only the article before it changes: *i loro studi* (their studies).

checkQuiz.question: How do you say 'their findings'?
checkQuiz.explanation: 'loro' never changes; the plural article 'i' matches 'risultati'.

lessons.title: Quantifiers & Numbers
lessons.subtitle: Molto, poco, tutto, ogni, alcuni, primo, secondo.
lessons.mentalModel: Quantifiers establish scope: *alcuni studi* (some studies), *tutti i dati* (all data), *il primo capitolo* (the first chapter).
lessons.bridgeMarker: YDS Note: Watch out for 'ogni' vs 'tutti'. 'Ogni' is followed by a singular noun (*ogni ricercatore*), while 'tutti' takes plural (*tutti i ricercatori*).

checkQuiz.question: Which quantifier is invariable and takes a singular noun?
